profile.name: Leopold Aschenbrenner
profile.hook: The OpenAI researcher who built a $9 billion AI fund
profile.dek: I trace his path from Columbia valedictorian and OpenAI researcher to a $9.28 billion AI hedge fund, then show what the SEC filings reveal about his stake and what they do not.
profile.answer: Leopold Aschenbrenner net worth is not publicly established. He owns 50% to 75% of Situational Awareness LP, an AI-focused hedge fund adviser that reported $9.28 billion in regulatory assets in June 2026, but no filing shows his personal fortune.

wealth.basis: Owns 50% to 75% of the adviser, but personal capital, fee income and liabilities are not disclosed
wealth.paragraph: Leopold Aschenbrenner’s net worth is not publicly established as of October 27, 2026. What the filings do show is ownership. The firm’s [June 2026 Form ADV](https://reports.adviserinfo.sec.gov/reports/ADV/333011/PDF/333011.pdf) lists him as chief investment officer and a limited partner owning 50% to 75% of Situational Awareness LP, the adviser, and 75% or more of its general partner. The adviser reported $9.28 billion in regulatory assets, and its [Schedule 13D filings](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583625000543/xslSCHEDULE_13D_X01/primary_doc.xml) say it earns fees based on assets and on realized and unrealized gains. A stake in a fast-growing adviser like that can be very valuable, but the filings disclose neither the fee rates, the fund’s returns, his own capital in the fund nor his liabilities. Without those, any dollar figure would be a guess, so I publish none.

sections.heading: Who is Leopold Aschenbrenner?
paragraphs: Aschenbrenner grew up in Germany and graduated as valedictorian of Columbia at 19, according to the introduction to his [June 2024 Dwarkesh Podcast interview](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/leopold-aschenbrenner). His [own biography](https://situational-awareness.ai/leopold-aschenbrenner/) says he then researched long-run economic growth at Oxford’s Global Priorities Institute and later joined OpenAI’s Superalignment team. He lives in San Francisco.

He left OpenAI in April 2024. In the same interview he said OpenAI told employees he was fired for leaking, which he said referred to a brainstorming document he had shared with three outside researchers for feedback. He also said he had been told a memo he wrote warning that OpenAI’s security was inadequate was a reason. That is his account; OpenAI’s internal reasoning is not public.

The two research subjects explain the fund. Growth research asks what can change the scale of the economy; alignment research asks whether powerful AI can be controlled. His investment thesis joins them: if AI keeps improving quickly, the companies that supply chips, memory, data centers and power may gain before the final winners are known. Readers interested in his former employer can see our [OpenAI ownership investigation](/who-owns-chatgpt-openai/).

sections.heading: Situational Awareness: from an essay to a $9 billion fund
paragraphs: His [June 2024 Situational Awareness essay series](https://situational-awareness.ai/) set out a forecast about AI capabilities, industrial expansion and security, and his biography names Patrick Collison, John Collison, Nat Friedman and Daniel Gross as anchor investors in the firm. The [firm’s website](https://situationalawarenesslp.com/) dates its founding to September 2024 and describes a global equity strategy across technology and energy.

Growth since then is visible in SEC filings. The [first Form 13F](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583625000120/xslForm13F_X02/primary_doc.xml), for December 31, 2024, listed $254.8 million of securities. By June 30, 2026 the table showed $20.24 billion. The more reliable size measure is the [Form ADV](https://reports.adviserinfo.sec.gov/reports/ADV/333011/PDF/333011.pdf) filed June 11, 2026: $9,278,344,000 in regulatory assets across two accounts. Its main fund, Situational Awareness Partners LP, which has an offshore feeder, had 81 investors and a $5 million minimum investment, and the adviser had eight employees.

The same Form ADV shows who owns the business. Aschenbrenner, listed as chief investment officer and a limited partner, owns 50% to 75% of the adviser. Carl Shulman, director of research and co-portfolio manager, owns 25% to 50%, and chief operating officer Nicholas Gross-Whitaker 5% to 10%. Aschenbrenner also owns 75% or more of Situational Awareness LLC, the adviser’s general partner, and the firm’s [Schedule 13D filings](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583625000543/xslSCHEDULE_13D_X01/primary_doc.xml) describe him as its control person.

The firm also takes large stakes in single companies. It reported 5.8% of Core Scientific in August 2025, raised to 9.4% that October before falling to 4.4% by July 2026, 5.6% of Nebius in May 2026 and 21.1% of [SharonAI Holdings](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583626000468/xslSCHEDULE_13D_X02/primary_doc.xml) in August 2026. Those filings say the adviser is paid fees based on assets under management and on realized and unrealized gains.

sections.heading: An AI thesis expressed through listed infrastructure
paragraphs: The [June 30, 2026 information table](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583626000418/xslForm13F_X02/form13fInfoTable.xml) gives a concrete view of the disclosed strategy. It includes memory suppliers, chip-related businesses, data-center and computing infrastructure, and energy businesses. This is a quarter-end view of reportable securities; it is not a live list of everything the manager owns.

My reading is that the portfolio expresses an AI buildout thesis through several supply-chain bottlenecks rather than only through model developers. A business can benefit from demand for compute without owning a frontier model. That also creates an important risk: different holdings may depend on the same spending cycle, so having several company names does not necessarily mean having several independent sources of return.

A holdings filing cannot settle whether that risk was hedged. The [SEC’s Form 13F guidance](https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/staff-guidance/frequently-asked-questions-about-form-13f) excludes short positions and explains that an option entry refers to the underlying security. A large put entry is therefore not the premium paid for insurance. Without the terms and the rest of the book, I cannot reconstruct the manager’s net exposure from the table alone.

sections.heading: My finding: two memory stocks explain much of the disclosed table
paragraphs: I checked the June table against its cover-page total. It reports SanDisk at $5,673,738,513 and Micron at $5,573,819,392. Adding the two produces $11,247,557,905. Dividing by the [reported $20,242,292,228 table total](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583626000418/xslForm13F_X02/primary_doc.xml) gives 55.6%, rounded to one decimal. This is a reproducible concentration measure within the disclosed 13F table, not 55.6% of his personal assets or necessarily of the fund’s net asset value.

The denominator matters because the table includes option-underlying values alongside ordinary share positions. Calling the whole total cash invested would misread the filing. My calculation deliberately describes the reported table and leaves the fund’s unreported positions, borrowing and liabilities outside its scope.

The two cover pages also show the number of reported entries falling from 42 in March to 26 in June while reported table value rises from $13.68 billion to $20.24 billion. That does not demonstrate a corresponding investment return: new capital, position changes and option reporting can all affect the comparison. Entries are not a count of distinct companies, either; a company can appear separately for shares and options.

The practical lesson for a financial investigator is to preserve the unit at every step. Company market capitalization measures a company. A securities table measures disclosed positions under a reporting rule. Fund net asset value measures investor capital after the relevant liabilities. Personal net worth measures one person’s assets less liabilities. A number can be accurate in its original unit and misleading when relabeled.

profile.methodology: I conduct independent document-based research for Visionary Talks. For this profile I read every Form 13F the firm has filed, its June 2026 Form ADV, its Schedule 13D and 13G filings, the founder’s own biography and essays, the firm’s website and his June 2024 podcast interview. I calculated concentration and growth figures directly from reported dollar values. Reported holdings, regulatory assets, first-person statements and my interpretation are identified separately. These records do not provide a personal balance sheet, fee rates or audited returns, so I do not turn managed assets into a personal wealth estimate. The research check date is October 27, 2026; financial observations keep their own dates.
notes: No verified personal net-worth observations were established; no historical personal-wealth graph is drawn.
The earlier $400M to $1.6B estimate on this page was an assumption-based model, not a verified dollar range.
Form ADV ownership is reported in bands, not exact percentages.
13F totals include option positions at underlying value and exclude short positions, so they differ from regulatory assets.

faq.question: What is Leopold Aschenbrenner’s net worth?
faq.answer: It is not publicly established as of October 27, 2026. He owns 50% to 75% of Situational Awareness LP, which reported $9.28 billion in regulatory assets in June 2026, but no filing discloses his fee income, his own capital in the fund or his liabilities.

faq.question: Who is Leopold Aschenbrenner?
faq.answer: He is a German-born former OpenAI Superalignment researcher who wrote the June 2024 Situational Awareness essays on AI and then founded Situational Awareness LP, an AI-focused investment firm in San Francisco, in September 2024.

faq.question: How much money does Situational Awareness manage?
faq.answer: $9,278,344,000 in regulatory assets, according to the firm’s Form ADV filed June 11, 2026. Its 13F table showed $20.24 billion at June 30, 2026, but that figure counts option positions at the value of the underlying shares, so it is not money under management.

faq.question: Why was Leopold Aschenbrenner fired from OpenAI?
faq.answer: He said on the Dwarkesh Podcast in June 2024 that OpenAI told staff he was fired for leaking, which he said referred to a brainstorming document he shared with three outside researchers. He also said he was told a memo he had written on OpenAI security was a reason. That is his account.

faq.question: Is Leopold Aschenbrenner a billionaire?
faq.answer: No source establishes that. His majority stake in a $9.28 billion adviser could be worth a great deal, but a firm’s assets belong to its investors, and the value of his stake depends on undisclosed fees and profits.

faq.question: What stocks does Situational Awareness own?
faq.answer: Its June 30, 2026 Form 13F listed 26 entries led by SanDisk and Micron, followed by Bloom Energy, TSMC, Nebius and CoreWeave. It has also reported large stakes in Core Scientific, Nebius and SharonAI.
